title: The Long-Duration Continuity Layer
editorialBoundary: This model investigates mechanisms that can preserve power longer than individual governments, companies, empires or religious administrations. Longevity is not proof of secret coordination, criminality or a single hidden ruler.
thesis: The deepest durable power is rarely a name alone. It is a transferable mechanism: succession rights, property law, archives, credit, appointment authority, coercive institutions, technical standards, land, infrastructure, education, data and legitimacy. Families and individuals matter when they can inherit, appoint, own, veto or reproduce those mechanisms.

layers.name: Succession and Appointment Rights
layers.description: The ability to decide who occupies the next office, board seat, trusteeship, command or leadership role.
layers.survivalMechanism: Constitutions, hereditary rules, voting agreements, nomination rights, trustee powers and cadre systems.
layers.falsePositiveRisk: Family presence or social access without an enforceable appointment right.

layers.name: Property, Voting and Beneficial Control
layers.description: Control that survives because assets, votes or veto rights pass through trusts, foundations, holding companies or dynastic ownership vehicles.
layers.survivalMechanism: Voting shares, dual-class stock, foundations, trusts, partnerships, land titles and debt covenants.
layers.falsePositiveRisk: Confusing custody, passive investment or assets under management with ownership.

layers.name: Credit, Liquidity and Collateral
layers.description: The capacity to finance states, firms and crises or to deny funding when alternatives are limited.
layers.survivalMechanism: Central-bank mandates, sovereign debt markets, banking relationships, private credit, collateral rules and lender networks.
layers.falsePositiveRisk: Assuming every creditor can dictate policy or caused a crisis from which it benefited.

layers.name: Law, Jurisdiction and Enforcement
layers.description: The power to define ownership, contracts, sanctions, liability, market access and the legitimacy of other forms of power.
layers.survivalMechanism: Courts, legal codes, treaty systems, regulatory mandates, professional bars and enforcement agencies.
layers.falsePositiveRisk: Treating lawyers, judges or advisers as a single coordinated bloc.

layers.name: Security, Intelligence and Coercive Continuity
layers.description: The institutional ability to gather privileged information, protect systems, impose force or survive political transitions.
layers.survivalMechanism: Military commands, intelligence services, police powers, classified networks, alliances and contractor ecosystems.
layers.falsePositiveRisk: Inferring command from former service, security clearance or association alone.

layers.name: Infrastructure, Standards and Technical Dependence
layers.description: Control of the rails others must use: payments, cloud, chips, ports, energy, telecoms, identity and technical standards.
layers.survivalMechanism: Network effects, patents, specialist knowledge, capital intensity, interoperability rules and long-term contracts.
evidenceRequired: Demonstrated ability to deny or delay access
layers.falsePositiveRisk: Equating a leading market share with permanent monopoly or total control.

layers.name: Archives, Data and Information Asymmetry
layers.description: The ability to preserve, classify, discover, filter or distribute information that shapes decisions and historical memory.
layers.survivalMechanism: State archives, intelligence holdings, proprietary datasets, media distribution, search systems and institutional recordkeeping.
layers.falsePositiveRisk: Assuming possession of information proves manipulation or coordinated censorship.

layers.name: Education, Credentialing and Elite Reproduction
layers.description: The ability to select, train, certify and network future officials, executives, experts and gatekeepers.
layers.survivalMechanism: Universities, fellowships, professional credentials, academies, recruitment pipelines and alumni networks.
layers.falsePositiveRisk: Treating shared education or club membership as proof of a conspiracy.

layers.name: Legitimacy, Tradition and Sacred Authority
layers.description: Narratives and institutions that make rule appear lawful, natural, moral or divinely sanctioned across generations.
layers.survivalMechanism: Constitutions, monarchy, civic ritual, religious offices, customary law, philanthropy and cultural institutions.
layers.falsePositiveRisk: Treating a religion, ethnicity or culture as one actor or assuming belief automatically produces political command.

layers.name: Crisis Adaptation and Institutional Conversion
layers.description: The capacity to survive regime change by converting family, financial or institutional power into a new legal form.
layers.survivalMechanism: Diversification, jurisdictional mobility, foundations, corporate restructuring, alliances and professional management.
layers.falsePositiveRisk: Retrofitting continuity onto unrelated entities that share only a name or symbolism.

investigationQuestions: Who can appoint or remove the operator?
Who owns the voting right rather than merely the economic exposure?
Who holds the archive, licence, standard, key, collateral or legal jurisdiction?
What survives when the public leader, government, religion or corporate brand changes?
Can the mechanism be inherited, delegated or transferred without public attention?
Which independent institutions can veto or constrain it?
What documented outcome proves that access became action?
What evidence would show that the alleged hidden hand is actually fragmented or absent?

evolutionPolicy.historicalArchive: Every published change must preserve the prior mechanism, score, evidence and conclusion.
